stem: A 30-year-old woman had a molar pregnancy several months ago. Her beta-hCG is rising again, and she has hemoptysis with multiple lung nodules on chest imaging. A uterine biopsy shows sheets of malignant cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, with extensive hemorrhage and necrosis. No chorionic villi are present.
oneliner: 30F + molar pregnancy months ago + rising hCG + hemoptysis + lung nodules + sheets of trophoblast, hemorrhage, no villi → which lesion?

whyNot.B: Has **swollen chorionic villi**; here **no villi** are present
whyNot.C: A mole that **invades the myometrium but still shows villi**
whyNot.D: Made of **intermediate trophoblast**, with a **low hCG** and no biphasic sheets
whyNot.E: Benign **abnormal attachment**, with normal villi and no malignant trophoblast

why: Choriocarcinoma is **malignant cytotrophoblast plus syncytiotrophoblast** in sheets with **hemorrhage and no villi**. It makes **very high hCG** and spreads early by blood to the **lungs**.

idea.rule: No villi plus malignant trophoblast = choriocarcinoma; villi present means mole.
also: Complete mole: 50% of gestational choriocarcinomas follow it
Can occur in the testis as a germ cell tumor

stem: A 45-year-old multiparous woman has heavy, painful periods. The uterus is diffusely enlarged, soft and globular, and ultrasound shows no ovarian cyst. Hysterectomy tissue shows endometrial glands and stroma deep within the myometrium.
oneliner: 45F + multiparous + heavy painful periods + diffuse boggy globular uterus + no ovarian cyst + glands in myometrium → which lesion?
ask: Which lesion best fits the findings?

whyNot.A: Endometrial tissue **outside the uterus** (ovaries, peritoneum), with adhesions and pelvic pain
whyNot.B: A **discrete firm smooth-muscle mass** with a whorled cut surface, giving an **asymmetric** uterus
whyNot.C: **Crowded glands within the endometrium**, not in the myometrium
whyNot.E: An **ovarian chocolate cyst**; none was seen on ultrasound

why: **Adenomyosis** is **endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium**. It enlarges the uterus **diffusely and symmetrically**, causing **menorrhagia and dysmenorrhea** in older multiparous women.

idea.rule: Endometrial tissue in the myometrium = adenomyosis; outside the uterus = endometriosis.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has an ill-defined breast mass. Core biopsy shows small uniform cells infiltrating in single-file rows and growing in a targetoid pattern around ducts. Immunostaining for E-cadherin is negative.
oneliner: 60F + ill-defined breast mass + single-file small uniform cells + targetoid growth + E-cadherin negative → which tumor?

options.A: Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type

whyNot.A: Forms **cohesive glands or nests** and is **E-cadherin positive**
whyNot.B: A **benign** tumor with bloody nipple discharge, with a fibrovascular core
whyNot.D: **Syncytial sheets** of high-grade cells with a prominent **lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate** and a pushing border
whyNot.E: **Clusters of cells floating in pools of mucin**

why: **Loss of E-cadherin** makes lobular cells **discohesive**, so they spread as **single-file rows** and around ducts in a **targetoid** pattern. It is often **bilateral and multicentric**.

idea.rule: No E-cadherin means no cell cohesion, so the cells line up in single file.
also: Lobular carcinoma in situ: same E-cadherin loss
Metastasizes to unusual sites (GI tract, ovary)

stem: A 33-year-old woman with infertility has an endometrial biopsy. It shows tortuous glands with secretions, coiled spiral arteries and an edematous, decidualized stroma.
oneliner: 33F + infertility + biopsy with tortuous secretory glands + coiled spiral arteries + decidualized stroma → which hormone?

whyNot.A: Drives the **proliferative phase**: straight glands without secretions
whyNot.C: Triggers **ovulation** and luteinization; it does not act directly on the endometrial glands
whyNot.D: Stimulates **follicle growth** and estrogen; it does not drive the glandular secretions
whyNot.E: An androgen that does not produce this **secretory** pattern

why: After ovulation the **corpus luteum** secretes **progesterone**. It converts proliferative endometrium into the **secretory phase**: coiled glands with secretions, **coiled spiral arteries** and decidualized stroma.

idea.rule: Estrogen builds the endometrium, progesterone ripens it.
also: Progesterone falls if no pregnancy, causing menses
hCG maintains the corpus luteum in pregnancy
Luteal phase is a fixed 14 days

stem: A 32-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles has an endometrial biopsy. It shows long, straight tubular glands with empty lumens in an abundant stroma. The spiral arteries are not coiled.
oneliner: 32F + regular 28-day cycle + straight tubular glands + empty lumens + abundant stroma + uncoiled arteries → which phase?

whyNot.B: Shows **subnuclear vacuoles** in the glands, not empty straight lumens
whyNot.C: **Saw-toothed, tortuous glands** with secretions and **decidualized stroma**
whyNot.D: **Shedding of the functional layer** with hemorrhage and glandular breakdown
whyNot.E: **Decidualized stroma** with enlarged glands (Arias-Stella change), not straight empty glands

why: Before ovulation, **estrogen from the developing follicle** drives **straight tubular glands** with **empty lumens** in a thick stroma. The **secretions** and **coiled arteries** only appear after ovulation under progesterone.

idea.rule: Straight and empty = proliferative; coiled and secreting = secretory.
